papers.title: Acceptance and commitment therapy for schizophrenia and psychosis inpatients with recovery and experience orientation (ASPIRE): A qualitative study of participant experiences.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This uncontrolled study aims to gather a comprehensive understanding of participants' experiences during an inpatient intervention specialized in the treatment of psychotic disorders, embedded in a holistic therapeutic ward-concept rooted in acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), extending its isolated delivery in group therapies. Particular attention was paid to participants' perceptions of the concept, the mechanisms of impact they described and the transfer of therapy-related experiences into daily life. DESIGN: A qualitative study design was used to evaluate experiences. METHODS: Thirty semi-structured interviews were conducted with inpatients with psychosis upon completing the intervention. Following a later protocol amendment, 11 complementary follow-up interviews were conducted. All were audio-recorded and transcribed. A Straussian grounded theory-informed content structuring analysis was carried out to create a comprehensive coding scheme. RESULTS: Participants regarded the general concept as fostering for their personal development, emphasizing positive interactions with staff and other inpatients, while pointing out structural barriers. Group therapies were perceived as highly relevant, engaging and practical in nature. Reported impacts represent the established ACT-domains 'open', 'aware' and 'active'. Meaningful transfers to daily life were prevalent at both times of interviews, and participants generally displayed an optimistic and life-oriented attitude half a year upon completion. CONCLUSIONS: The holistic therapeutic concept appears to succeed in impactfully conveying the principles of ACT. Findings suggest that through including the entire ward staff as ACT-therapists, it promotes therapeutic alliance and interpersonal connectedness to a particular degree. Participants highlighted the hands-on and guiding nature of therapy contents as especially motivating, leading to meaningful change.

papers.title: Effect of interventions for stress management on blood pressure changes in healthy adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Non-pharmacological therapy or lifestyle modification is recommended as a first-line approach to hypertension management. Chronic stress is a modifiable risk factor of hypertension through behavioral change. However, no prior studies have conducted a meta-analysis of stress management aimed at the primary prevention of hypertension in normotensive general population. We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane library for eligible trials, limited to English-language articles published up to October 2025. Studies involving healthy adults without hypertension that used interventions for stress management and reported blood pressure outcomes were included. Effect sizes were calculated as between-group mean differences in systolic and diastolic blood pressures change, and were pooled using a random-effects model. Twenty-two randomized controlled trials with a maximal total sample of 3089 individuals were included in the meta-analysis. Among the different types of intervention considered, a consistent reduction in systolic blood pressure (between-group mean difference (mmHg) [95% confidence interval]) compared with the control was found for mind-body exercise (-2.17 [-3.29, -1.05]); for meditation (-1.49 [-2.67, -0.31]); and for relaxation (-4.76 [-8.48, -1.04]). Similarly, reductions in diastolic blood pressure were found with values of -1.69 [-2.81, -0.56]; -1.00 [-1.84, -0.15]; and -1.71 [-3.99, 0.56], respectively. Interventions for stress management may lower systolic and diastolic blood pressures in normotensive general population. It is possible that stress management contributes to reduce future cardiovascular risk.

papers.title: Cognitive Strategy Use for Functional Compensation in Multiple Sclerosis: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To examine the evidence supporting the use of specific compensatory cognitive strategies in people with multiple sclerosis (PwMS). DATA SOURCES: PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and CINAHL were queried using an optimized string with Medical Subject Headings search terms to identify English language articles published through December 31, 2024. STUDY SELECTION: Clinical trials and observations studies (eg, cohort and case-control studies) were eligible if they included adults with PwMS who underwent an intervention with one or more defined cognitive strategies. Included studies had at least one subjective or objective quantifiable cognitive outcome. Screening and eligibility checks were independently done by the first author and then reviewed by the senior author. DATA EXTRACTION: Study demographics, cognitive strategy information, and cognitive outcome data were extracted by one author and then verified by a second author. Studies were summarized using established evidence grading criteria and effect size estimates were calculated for each cognitive domain where a strategy was assessed. DATA SYNTHESIS: The most frequently used cognitive strategy in the 64 identified studies (n=3759) was visualization/imagery-based mnemonics (34.9%), followed by planning/organization strategies (28.6%), analog memory aids (19.0%), mental rehearsal strategies (15.9%), and mindfulness (15.9%). Small-to-medium improvements in objective and subjective learning and memory were observed with several attentional, internal memory, and external memory strategies that were used alone and in combination. Attentional and relaxation-based strategies were also associated with significant small effects on processing speed. CONCLUSIONS: Several cognitive strategies have been examined in PwMS, with visualization/imagery-based mnemonics having the highest usage and subsequent supporting evidence. These findings can support clinicians when determining which approaches to include in a cognitive rehabilitation program for PwMS.
